topics.title: 1.1 Basic terms
topics.content:
- Data: raw facts (e.g., 25, "Zara", 9.5).

- Data item / field: the smallest named unit. Example: Name .

- Record: a collection of related fields. Example: Student(RollNo, Name, Marks).

- File: a collection of records.

- Entity and attribute: an entity is something with properties; an attribute is one

- property. Entity = Student, attributes = RollNo, Name, Marks.

```
  FILE (Students)
   ├── RECORD 1 : [ RollNo=101 | Name=Zara | Marks=88 ]
   ├── RECORD 2 : [ RollNo=102 | Name=Arun | Marks=75 ]
   └── RECORD 3 : [ RollNo=103 | Name=Mia          | Marks=92 ]
            ▲                ▲            ▲
         field          field           field
```

topics.title: 1.2 What is a data structure?
topics.content:
A data structure is a way of storing and organising data in memory so that it can be used

#### efficiently. It has two parts

- 1. Organisation: how items are arranged in memory.

- 2. Operations: what you can do (insert, delete, search, traverse, sort, merge).

Classification

```
                             DATA STRUCTURES
                         /                     \

               PRIMITIVE                      NON-PRIMITIVE
          (int, float, char, bool)            /           \
                                     LINEAR             NON-LINEAR
                               (Array, Linked List,      (Tree, Graph)
                                Stack, Queue)


    Linear: elements form a sequence; each has one predecessor and one successor.
    Non-linear: an element can connect to many others.
    Static vs dynamic: size fixed at compile time (arrays) versus growing and shrinking at
    run time (linked lists).
```

topics.title: 1.3 Abstract Data Type (ADT)
topics.content:
An ADT describes what a structure does (values and operations) without saying how it is implemented. [AHU] defines an ADT as a mathematical model with a collection of operations defined on it.

```
  ADT                Operations (the interface)               Possible implementations

  Stack              push, pop, peek, isEmpty                 array, linked list

  Queue              enqueue, dequeue, front                  circular array, linked list

  List               insert, delete, search                   array, linked list

  Dictionary         insert, delete, lookup                   hash table, BST
```

Analogy: a TV remote is an interface. You don't need to know the circuits inside.

topics.title: 1.4 What is an algorithm?
topics.content:
A finite sequence of well-defined steps that solves a problem. Five properties:

- 1. Input: zero or more.

- 2. Output: at least one.

- 3. Definiteness: each step is unambiguous.

- 4. Finiteness: it stops after finitely many steps.

- 5. Effectiveness: each step is simple enough to be carried out.

topics.title: 1.5 Writing algorithms the Lipschutz way
topics.content:
Algorithm 1.1: Find the largest element of an array DATA with N elements

```
 1. [Initialise]     Set MAX := DATA[1], K := 2.
 2. Repeat Steps 3 and 4 while K <= N:
 3.      If MAX < DATA[K], then: Set MAX := DATA[K].
 4.      Set K := K + 1.
 5. Write: MAX.
 6. Exit.
```

#### Python version

```
 def find_max(data):
      mx = data[0]
      for x in data[1:]:
            if x > mx:
                mx = x
      return mx
```

#### Flowchart symbols (text form)

```
   ( Start/End )     [ Process ]    < Decision? >       /Input-Output/
```

#### Flowchart of Algorithm 1.1

```
   (Start) → [MAX=DATA[1], K=2] → <K <= N?> ──No──→ /Print MAX/ → (End)
                                         │Yes
                                         ▼
                              <MAX < DATA[K]?> ─Yes→ [MAX=DATA[K]]
                                         │No                    │
                                         └────────┬─────────┘
                                                    ▼
                                                [K = K+1] ──→ (back to K <= N?)
```

topics.title: 1.6 Four stages of problem solving
topics.content:
- 1. Understand the problem: input, output, constraints.

- 2. Plan: pick a data structure and an algorithm.

- 3. Implement: write the code.

- 4. Review: test with normal, edge and large cases, and check the cost.

- Confusing a data structure (the storage layout) with an algorithm (the procedure).

- Starting to code before understanding the input and output.

- Ignoring edge cases such as an empty array or a single element.

### Code Problem 4 (Easy): Sum of digits (algorithm-writing practice)

**Statement:** Write a numbered-step algorithm (Lipschutz style) and code to find the sum of digits of N. Algorithm: 1. Set SUM := 0. 2. Repeat while N > 0: SUM := SUM + (N mod 10); N := N div 10. 3. Write SUM. 4. Exit.

**Example:** 4521 → 12. Complexity: O(log₁₀ n).

```python
def digit_sum(n):
    s = 0
    while n > 0:
          s += n % 10
          n //= 10
    return s
```

topics.title: 2.1 Why analyse?
topics.content: Running time depends on the machine, language and input, so we count basic operations as a function of input size n. We ignore constants and keep the dominant term.

topics.title: 2.2 Time and space complexity
topics.content:
- Time complexity T(n): number of basic steps.

- Space complexity S(n): extra memory used besides the input.

topics.title: 2.3 Cases (Lipschutz: best, average, worst)
topics.content:
Example: linear search for ITEM in an array of n elements.

```
 Case                       Meaning                               Comparisons

 Best                       Item at position 1                    1

 Average                    Item uniformly anywhere               (n+1)/2

 Worst                      Last position or absent               n
```

We usually quote the worst case because it is a guarantee.

topics.title: 2.4 Asymptotic notation
topics.content:
- O(g(n)) is an upper bound: f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for n ≥ n₀.

- Ω(g(n)) is a lower bound.

- Θ(g(n)) is a tight bound (both O and Ω).

```
  cost
    │                                      c·g(n) ← upper bound
    │                                 ╱╱
    │                           ╱╱     ·    f(n)
    │                     ╱╱    ·
    │                ╱╱ ·
    │          ╱╱·
    │    ╱╱·     ← after n0, f(n) stays below c·g(n)
    └───────────┬──────────────────── n
                     n0
```

Rules

- 1. Drop constants: 5n → O(n).

- 2. Drop lower-order terms: n² + n + 7 → O(n²).

- 3. Sequential blocks add: O(n) + O(n²) → O(n²).

- 4. Nested loops multiply: n × n → O(n²).

topics.title: 2.5 Growth-rate ladder
topics.content:
```
 Slowest growth (best)                                       Fastest growth (worst)
 O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n³) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)
```

#### Operations needed (approximate)

```
  n                log₂ n        n log₂ n        n²            2ⁿ

  10               3             33              100           1,024

  100              7             664             10,000        1.3×10³⁰

  1,000            10            9,966           1,000,000     ∞ (practically)
```

#### Text graph (cost against n)

```
 cost
   │ 2ⁿ │               n²
   │      │        ╱
   │      │    ╱       n log n
   │      │╱   ╱─────
   │      ╱╱──────── n
   │ ──────────────── log n
   │ ═════════════════ 1
   └────────────────────── n
```

topics.title: 2.7 Space complexity
topics.content:
- Sum of an array with one loop variable: O(1) extra space.

- Building a copy of the array: O(n) extra space.

- Recursion depth d uses O(d) stack space (more in Module 5).

topics.title: 2.8 Time–space trade-off
topics.content:
You can often be faster by using more memory. Example: precompute a lookup table to answer queries in O(1), costing O(n) space.

#### Common Mistakes

- Saying O(2n) is different from O(n). It is not.

- Treating best-case as the cost.

- Forgetting that a + b on huge numbers or strings may not be O(1).

#### Quick Revision

Big-O means "no worse than". Drop constants and small terms. A loop that halves or

doubles gives log n. Nested loops multiply.

### Code Problem 3 (Easy): Sum 1..n three ways

**Statement:** Compute 1 + 2 + … + n by (a) a loop, (b) the formula, (c) recursion. State each complexity.

```python
def loop_sum(n):
     s = 0
     for i in range(1, n + 1): s += i

     return s                                      # O(n) time, O(1) space


def formula_sum(n):
     return n * (n + 1) // 2                       # O(1)

     return 0 if n == 0 else n + rec_sum(n - 1)                 # O(n) time, O(n) stack
```

topics.title: 3.1 Linear array
topics.content:
A list of n items of the same type, stored in consecutive memory locations, accessed by an index (subscript).

```
 Index :      0      1        2         3      4
            ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
   DATA     │ 12   │ 45   │       7   │ 33   │ 90     │

             └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
  Address: 1000         1004    1008   1012       1016     (4 bytes per int)
```

Terms (Lipschutz): LB (lower bound), UB (upper bound), length = UB − LB + 1.

topics.title: 3.2 Address calculation
topics.content:
```
  LOC(DATA[K]) = Base(DATA) + w × (K − LB)
```

where w = size of one element. Example: Base = 1000, w = 4, LB = 0, K = 3 → 1000 + 4×3 = 1012. This formula is why access by index is O(1).

topics.title: 3.3 Operations and costs
topics.content:
Traversal. Visit every element: O(n).

Insertion (Algorithm 3.1: insert ITEM at position K in LA with N elements)

```
  1. Set J := N.
  2. Repeat Steps 3 and 4 while J >= K:
  3.        Set LA[J+1] := LA[J].                   (move element down)
  4.        Set J := J - 1.
  5. Set LA[K] := ITEM.
  6. Set N := N + 1.
  7. Exit.



  Insert 20 at index 2 :
  before: [12][45][ 7][33][90][               ]
  shift :     12   45     ─►7    ─►33 ─►90                (move right, last to first)
  after : [12][45][20][ 7][33][90]
```

Deletion is the reverse: shift left, O(n).

```
  def insert(a, k, item):                         # a is a Python list used as a fixed array
        a.append(None)
        for j in range(len(a) - 1, k, -1):
             a[j] = a[j - 1]
        a[k] = item


  def delete(a, k):
        for j in range(k, len(a) - 1):

               a[j] = a[j + 1]
        a.pop()



  Operation                                     Best         Worst

  Access by index                               O(1)         O(1)

  Search (unsorted)                             O(1)         O(n)

  Insert at end                                 O(1)         O(1) (if space)

  Insert at middle or front                     O(1)         O(n)

  Delete                                        O(1)         O(n)
```

topics.title: 3.4 Two-dimensional arrays
topics.content:
A table with rows and columns: A[i][j] .

```
               col0       col1       col2
 row0      [    1     |    2     |    3     ]
 row1      [    4     |    5     |    6     ]
 row2      [    7     |    8     |    9     ]
```

Row-major order (C, Python, Java): row 0, then row 1, ... LOC(A[i][j]) = Base + w × (i × COLS + j) Column-major order (Fortran): column 0, then column 1, ... LOC(A[i][j]) = Base + w × (j × ROWS + i)

Example: 3×3, Base = 2000, w = 2, row-major, A[2][1] → 2000 + 2×(2×3+1) = 2014.

topics.title: 3.5 Records
topics.content:
A record groups fields of different types.

```
 class Student:
        def __init__(self, roll, name, marks):
               self.roll, self.name, self.marks = roll, name, marks


 students = [Student(101, "Zara", 88), Student(102, "Arun", 75)]          # array of records
```

topics.title: 3.6 Pointers (idea)
topics.content:
A pointer stores the address of another variable. Pointers make linked structures possible (Module 7).

topics.content:
- Prefix sums: pre[i] = pre[i-1] + a[i] , so any range sum is pre[r] - pre[l-1] in

- O(1).

- Reverse in place: swap a[i] and a[n-1-i] .

- Rotate: reverse the whole array, then reverse the two parts.

#### Common Mistakes

- Off-by-one errors (index runs 0..n−1).

- Shifting in the wrong direction when inserting (overwrites data).

- Assuming a Python list is a fixed array. It is a dynamic array.

Arrays give O(1) index access thanks to the address formula. Insert and delete in the middle cost O(n) because of shifting. A 2D array is stored row by row (row-major).

### Code Problem 1 (Easy): Reverse an array in place

**Example:** [1,2,3,4,5] → [5,4,3,2,1]

```python
def reverse(a):
     i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
     while i < j:
          a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
          i += 1; j -= 1
     return a
```

**Complexity:** O(n) time, O(1) space.

### Code Problem 2 (Easy): Second largest element

**Statement:** Find the second largest distinct value in one pass.

**Example:** [12, 35, 1, 10, 34, 1] → 34

```python
def second_largest(a):
     first = second = float('-inf')
     for x in a:
          if x > first:
                first, second = x, first
          elif first > x > second:
                second = x

```

### Code Problem 3 (Medium): Rotate an array by k

**Statement:** Rotate right by k positions in place. Idea: reverse all, then reverse the first k and the rest. Complexity: O(n), O(1).

**Example:** [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] , k=3 → [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]

```python
def rotate(a, k):
     n = len(a); k %= n
     def rev(i, j):
          while i < j:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]; i += 1; j -= 1
     rev(0, n - 1); rev(0, k - 1); rev(k, n - 1)
     return a
```

### Code Problem 4 (Medium): Range sum queries (prefix sums)

**Statement:** Answer many queries sum(l, r) quickly.

```python
def build(a):
     pre = [0]
     for x in a: pre.append(pre[-1] + x)
     return pre


def range_sum(pre, l, r):                # inclusive, 0-based
     return pre[r + 1] - pre[l]


pre = build([2, 4, 5, 7, 1])
print(range_sum(pre, 1, 3))              # 16
```

**Complexity:** build O(n), each query O(1).

### Code Problem 5 (Easy): Transpose a matrix

```python
def transpose(m):
     r, c = len(m), len(m[0])
     return [[m[i][j] for i in range(r)] for j in range(c)]
# [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] -> [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]
```

**Complexity:** O(r·c).

A string is a finite sequence of characters. Stored as an array of characters (C: terminated by '\0' ; Python/Java: immutable objects).

topics.title: 5.1 Definition
topics.content:
A function is recursive if it calls itself with a smaller input. Every recursive solution needs:

- 1. Base case: a stopping condition with a direct answer.

- 2. Recursive case: moves toward the base case.

topics.title: 5.2 Factorial
topics.content:
n! = n × (n−1)!, with 0! = 1.

```
  def fact(n):
       if n == 0:               # base case
             return 1
       return n * fact(n - 1)        # recursive case
```

Call stack trace of fact(4)

```
  fact(4) → 4 * fact(3)
                    fact(3) → 3 * fact(2)
                                    fact(2) → 2 * fact(1)
                                                    fact(1) → 1 * fact(0)
                                                                    fact(0) → 1
  unwinding:     fact(1)=1 · fact(2)=2 · fact(3)=6 · fact(4)=24



  Call stack (top ↑)
   ┌─────────┐
   │ fact(0) │ ← top
   │ fact(1) │
   │ fact(2) │
   │ fact(3) │
   │ fact(4) │ ← bottom (first call)
   └─────────┘
```

Time O(n), space O(n) (stack depth).

topics.title: 5.3 Fibonacci
topics.content:
F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2).

```
 def fib(n):
        if n < 2: return n
        return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
```

Recursion tree for fib(5)

```
                            fib(5)
                        /            \
                   fib(4)            fib(3)
               /        \            /       \
         fib(3)       fib(2)    fib(2) fib(1)
         /     \
   fib(2) fib(1) ...
```

The same sub-problems are recomputed, giving O(2ⁿ). Fix: store results (memoization),

#### covered fully in Mastery (DP). Quick fix

```
 memo = {}
 def fib(n):
        if n < 2: return n
        if n not in memo:
              memo[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
        return memo[n]                      # now O(n)
```

topics.title: 5.4 Tower of Hanoi [L]
topics.content:
Move n disks from peg A to peg C using peg B; never place a larger disk on a smaller one.

```
 Procedure: Hanoi(n, A, C, B)
 1. If n = 1: move disk from A to C. Return.
 2. Hanoi(n-1, A, B, C)                          (move n-1 disks out of the way)
 3. Move disk n from A to C.
 4. Hanoi(n-1, B, C, A)                          (put them on top)
```

Moves required: 2ⁿ − 1. Time O(2ⁿ).

```
 n=2:        A: [1,2]        B: []        C: []
   move 1: A→B              A:[2]        B:[1]

   move 2: A→C       A:[]       B:[1]   C:[2]
   move 3: B→C       A:[]       B:[]    C:[1,2]
```

topics.title: 5.5 Other classic recursions
topics.content:
- Power: pow(x, n) = x * pow(x, n-1) is O(n); the smarter pow(x, n) = pow(x, n/2)²

- is O(log n).

- GCD (Euclid): gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) , with base gcd(a, 0) = a .

topics.title: 5.6 Recursion vs iteration
topics.content:
```
                    Recursion                                      Iteration

  Code              short, elegant                                 longer

  Space             O(depth) stack                                 O(1) usually

  Risk              stack overflow                                 none

  Best for          trees, divide and conquer                      simple repetition
```

Any recursion can be converted to a loop with an explicit stack.

- Missing or wrong base case (infinite recursion).

- Recursive call not moving closer to the base case.

- Using naïve Fibonacci for large n.

topics.content:

topics.title: 6.2 Binary search (sorted array only)
topics.content:
Compare with the middle and discard half each step.

```
 Find 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72]
  low=0 high=8 mid=4 → 16 < 23 → search right
  low=5 high=8 mid=6 → 38 > 23 → search left
  low=5 high=5 mid=5 → 23 ✓ found



 Algorithm 6.1 (Binary search) [L]
 1. Set BEG := LB, END := UB, MID := INT((BEG+END)/2).
 2. Repeat Steps 3 and 4 while BEG <= END and DATA[MID] != ITEM:
 3.      If ITEM < DATA[MID], set END := MID - 1.
         Else set BEG := MID + 1.
 4.      Set MID := INT((BEG+END)/2).
 5. If DATA[MID] = ITEM, set LOC := MID. Else set LOC := NULL.

 def binary_search(a, x):
      lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
      while lo <= hi:
          mid = (lo + hi) // 2
          if a[mid] == x: return mid
          if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
          else: hi = mid - 1
      return -1
```

Cost O(log n): 1,000,000 items need at most 20 comparisons.

topics.title: 6.3 Sorting basics

- Stable: equal items keep their original relative order.

Arrays need contiguous memory and O(n) shifting for insertion. A linked list stores each element in a separate node that holds data and a pointer to the next node.


topics.title: 9.3 Circular queue
topics.content:
Wrap the indices using modulo, so the array is treated as a ring.

```
               index 0
           ┌───┐
     4 ───┤      ├─── 1
           │     │
     3 ───┤      ├─── 2
           └───┘
   rear = (rear + 1) % N
   front = (front + 1) % N



 class CircularQueue:
      def __init__(self, n):
           self.a = [None]*n; self.n = n
           self.front = 0; self.size = 0
      def enqueue(self, x):
           if self.size == self.n: raise OverflowError
           self.a[(self.front + self.size) % self.n] = x
           self.size += 1
      def dequeue(self):
           if self.size == 0: raise IndexError
           x = self.a[self.front]
           self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.n
           self.size -= 1
           return x
```

Tracking size separates "full" from "empty" (both can have front == rear otherwise).

topics.title: 10.1 Tree terminology


A tree with n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges.

topics.title: 10.2 Binary trees
topics.content:
Each node has at most two children: left and right.

```
 class TreeNode:
      def __init__(self, v):
                   self.val = v; self.left = None; self.right = None
```

Types

- Full: each node has 0 or 2 children.

- Complete: all levels full except possibly the last, which fills left to right (heaps use this).

- Perfect: all leaves at the same depth; has 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.

- Skewed: every node has one child (behaves like a linked list).

Useful facts

- Maximum nodes at level i: 2ⁱ.

- Maximum nodes in a tree of height h: 2^(h+1) − 1.

- Minimum height with n nodes: ⌊log₂ n⌋.

topics.content:
Array (for complete trees): node at index i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and parent at ⌊(i−1)/2⌋.

A tree is a hierarchy with n−1 edges. The BST property makes search O(height). In-order on a BST is sorted. Balance matters.

### Code Problem 5 (Medium): BST insert and delete

```python
def insert(r, k):
     if r is None: return TreeNode(k)
     if k < r.val: r.left = insert(r.left, k)
     elif k > r.val: r.right = insert(r.right, k)
     return r


def delete(r, k):
     if r is None: return None
     if k < r.val: r.left = delete(r.left, k)
     elif k > r.val: r.right = delete(r.right, k)
     else:
         if not r.left: return r.right
         if not r.right: return r.left
         succ = r.right
         while succ.left: succ = succ.left
         r.val = succ.val
         r.right = delete(r.right, succ.val)
     return r
```

**Complexity:** O(h), where h is the height.

```python
            while cur: st.append(cur); cur = cur.left
            cur = st.pop(); k -= 1
            if k == 0: return cur.val
            cur = cur.right
```

topics.title: 11.1 Definitions [L, AHU]
topics.content:
A graph G = (V, E) has a set of vertices V and edges E.

```
 Undirected:                    Directed (digraph):             Weighted:
     A ─── B                        A ──► B                        A ─5─ B
     │      ╱ │                     ▲      │                       │        │ 2
     │ ╱      │                     │      ▼                       3        │
     C ─── D                        C ◄── D                        C ─4─ D



 Term                   Meaning

 Degree                 number of edges at a vertex (in-degree, out-degree for digraphs)

 Path                  sequence of vertices joined by edges

 Cycle                 path that starts and ends at the same vertex

 Connected             a path exists between every pair (undirected)

 Tree                  connected graph with no cycles

 DAG                   directed acyclic graph

 Complete graph        every pair of vertices connected: n(n−1)/2 edges
```

Sum of degrees = 2 × |E| (handshake lemma).

topics.title: 11.2 Representations
topics.content:
Graph: 0—1, 0—2, 1—2, 2—3

```
 Adjacency matrix                    Adjacency list
        0 1 2 3                      0: [1, 2]
   0    0 1 1 0                      1: [0, 2]
   1    1 0 1 0                      2: [0, 1, 3]
   2    1 1 0 1                      3: [2]
   3    0 0 1 0



                             Matrix                   List

 Space                       O(V²)                    O(V + E)

 Is edge (u,v)?              O(1)                     O(degree)

 List all neighbours         O(V)                     O(degree)

 Best for                    dense graphs             sparse graphs (most real ones)
```

topics.title: 11.3 Breadth-First Search (BFS)
topics.content:
Explore level by level using a queue.

```
 from collections import deque
 def bfs(adj, start):
        seen = {start}; q = deque([start]); order = []
        while q:

            u = q.popleft(); order.append(u)
            for v in adj[u]:
                 if v not in seen:
                       seen.add(v); q.append(v)
      return order



 Graph:      0 ── 1 ── 3
             │     │
             2 ── 4
 BFS from 0:      level0: 0 | level1: 1, 2 | level2: 3, 4         → order 0 1 2 3 4
```

Time O(V + E). In an unweighted graph, BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges).

topics.title: 11.4 Depth-First Search (DFS)
topics.content:
Go as deep as possible, then backtrack, using recursion or a stack.

```
 def dfs(adj, u, seen):
      seen.add(u)
      for v in adj[u]:
            if v not in seen:
                 dfs(adj, v, seen)



 DFS from 0 on the graph above (neighbours in ascending order):
  0 → 1 → 3 (dead end, back) → 4 → 2 → done              order: 0 1 3 4 2
```

Time O(V + E).

topics.title: 11.5 BFS vs DFS
topics.content:
```
                             BFS              DFS

 Data structure              Queue            Stack / recursion

 Explores                    by distance      by depth

 Shortest path
                             Yes              No
 (unweighted)

                             shortest hops,   cycle detection, connected components,
 Typical uses
                             levels           topological sort
```

topics.title: 11.6 Basic applications
topics.content:
- Connected components: run BFS/DFS from every unvisited vertex; count the runs.

- Cycle detection (undirected): DFS meets a visited vertex that is not its parent.

- Flood fill / islands in a grid: a grid is an implicit graph (4 or 8 neighbours).

- Maze solving, social-network "degrees of separation", web crawling.

#### Common Mistakes

- Forgetting the visited set (infinite loops on cycles).

- Marking visited when popping instead of when pushing in BFS (duplicate queue entries).

- Using a matrix for a huge sparse graph.

#### Quick Revision

Graph = vertices + edges. Use adjacency lists for sparse graphs. BFS (queue) gives shortest hops, DFS (stack) explores deep. Both are O(V+E).

topics.title: 12.1 Hashing
topics.content:
A hash function h(key) maps a key to an index of a table of size m.

```
  key "Zara" ──► h("Zara") = 17 mod 10 = 7
  table:    0 1 2 3 4 5 6 [7: Zara] 8 9
```

Goals: fast to compute, spreads keys uniformly. Common hash functions [L]

- Division: h(k) = k mod m (choose m prime).

- Mid-square: square the key, take the middle digits.

- Folding: split the key into parts and add them.

- Strings: h(s) = (s[0]·p⁰ + s[1]·p¹ + ...) mod m .

topics.title: 12.2 Collisions
topics.content:
Two different keys give the same index (inevitable, since there are more keys than slots). Chaining: each slot holds a linked list.

```
   0: ∅
   1: [11] → [21] → ∅
   2: [12] → ∅
   3: ∅
```

Open addressing (linear probing): if slot taken, try the next one.

```
 insert 11 (h=1) → slot 1
 insert 21 (h=1) → taken → slot 2
 insert 31 (h=1) → taken, taken → slot 3
```

Load factor α = n / m. Keep α below about 0.7, otherwise resize and rehash.

topics.title: 12.3 Cost
topics.content:
```
  Operation                                          Average         Worst (all collide)

  insert                                             O(1)            O(n)

  search                                             O(1)            O(n)

  delete                                             O(1)            O(n)

  Hash tables do not keep keys ordered.
```
